intro: “Will” is the best-known way to talk about the future, but it is not used for every future idea. We use it mainly for decisions made at the moment of speaking, offers, promises and predictions based on opinion.
objectifs: Form will / won't + base verb with every subject, in all forms.
Use will for an instant decision, an offer, a promise or a personal prediction.
Put probably, definitely and I think / I don't think in the right place with will.
Choose between will and be going to in common situations.

texte: “Will” is a modal verb: it is the same for every subject and it is followed by the base verb, without to. In speech and messages we use the short form 'll (I'll, you'll, she'll, it'll, we'll, they'll).

Negative: will not, short form “won't” (not “willn't”). Question: put will before the subject. Short answers: Yes, I will. / No, I won't. (Never use the short form in a positive short answer: “Yes, I will”, not “Yes, I'll”.)

lignes: Yes, subject + will. / No, subject + won't.
Yes, they will. / No, they won't.

texte: Use “will” when you decide at the moment you are speaking, with no plan before. This is the big difference from “be going to” (a decision made before, lesson 45).
We also use it to offer help, to promise, and to refuse (won't = doesn't want to / doesn't work).
exemples: It's cold in here. — I'll close the window.
Your bags look heavy. I'll help you.
I promise I won't tell anyone.
A refusal: the car doesn't work.

texte: Use “will” for a prediction based on opinion, belief or experience, often with I think, I'm sure, I hope, probably, maybe, perhaps, definitely.
We also use it for a future fact that is certain or official: “The shop will open at 9”, “I'll be 30 next year”.
exemples: I think it will be a great party.
Don't worry, you'll pass your exam.
The new metro line will open in 2027.

texte: Probably, definitely and certainly go AFTER will in the positive, but BEFORE won't in the negative: “He'll probably come” / “He probably won't come”.
For a negative opinion, English prefers “I don't think + will” to “I think + won't”: “I don't think it will rain” sounds more natural than “I think it won't rain”.
exemples: We'll definitely visit you in Quebec.
I don't think the bus will be on time.

sections.titre: Shall I / Shall we? and will or going to
texte: To offer help or make a suggestion as a question, British English uses “Shall I…?” and “Shall we…?”. American English usually says “Should I…?” or “Do you want me to…?”.
Summary: decision made now, offer, promise, opinion → will; plan already decided or visible evidence → be going to.

lignes: now: I'll have the fish, please.
before: I'm going to cook fish tonight.
opinion: I think Senegal will win.
evidence: Look, they're going to score!
I'll carry it. / Shall we go?

exemples: Shall I open the door for you?

formule: subject + will ('ll) + base verb · won't + base · Will + subject + base …?
prononciation: “I'll” is /aɪl/, “you'll” /juːl/, “we'll” /wiːl/: the final l is a “dark” l, with the tongue pulled back.
“won't” /wəʊnt/ (UK) / /woʊnt/ (US) is different from “want” /wɒnt/: I won't go ≠ I want to go.
In short answers, “will” is strong and stressed: Yes, I WILL /wɪl/.
erreurs: The negative short form is won't.
The phone is ringing. — I'm going to answer it.
The phone is ringing. — I'll answer it.
No short form in a positive short answer.
I don't think it will rain.
English puts the negative on think.
When I will arrive, I'll call you.
When I arrive, I'll call you.
After when (future meaning), use the present.

dialogue.contexte: In a small company in Abidjan, Marc and his colleague Grace are getting ready for an important meeting.
lignes: The clients arrive at ten. The meeting room isn't ready!
Don't panic. I'll set up the chairs.
Thanks. And the projector doesn't work.
I'll call the technician. Shall I order some coffee too?
Yes, please. Do you think they'll like our proposal?
I'm sure they will. It's a good offer.
I hope so. I don't think they'll accept the first price, though.
Then we'll negotiate. I promise it'll be fine.

mots: to say that you will certainly do something; a statement like this
to say you are happy to do or give something; a suggestion like this
I'll definitely come to your wedding.
What will you do in the future?
to think about problems and feel nervous
to give an answer without being sure; to think something is probably true

items: Don't worry, I ___ forget your birthday.
It's late. I think I ___ go to bed.
She's very ill, so she ___ come to work today.
Take an umbrella. It ___ probably rain.
I promise I ___ be late again.

exercices.consigne: Answer with I'll / Shall I…? (a decision or an offer).
items: I'll get you a glass of water. / Shall I get you a glass of water?
I'll turn on the light. / Shall I turn on the light?

exercices.consigne: Rewrite with the adverb in the right place.
items: I think it will snow. (make it negative)
I don't think it will snow.
Look at the clouds! It (will / is going to) rain.
I've decided: I (will / am going to) study medicine.
Oh, there's no milk. — I (will / am going to) buy some.
I think the film (will / is going to) be good.
will (both are possible; will is more natural for a simple opinion)

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: She will to travel next year.
Will you help me? — Yes, I'll.
Will you help me? — Yes, I will.
When she will arrive, we'll eat.

exercices.consigne: Write five predictions about your life or your country in ten years (with I think, probably, I don't think…).
items: In ten years, I think I'll speak English fluently. I'll probably live in Canada. I don't think I'll have a car, because I'll use public transport. Cameroon will definitely have more fast trains. Maybe I'll start my own company.

a_retenir: will ('ll) + base verb, the same for every subject; negative: won't.
Instant decision, offer, promise, refusal: will.
Prediction from opinion (I think, I'm sure, probably): will; with visible evidence: going to.
He'll probably… / He probably won't…; I don't think + will.
Shall I / Shall we…? to offer or suggest (British English).
